elements.quote: Background Health literacy responsiveness has been identified as a key action area in reducing the burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), which are a leading cause of death worldwide. Point-of-care (POC) testing has the potential to improve health literacy in individuals and communities.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the current state of knowledge (NCDs are a leading cause of death; health literacy responsiveness is key) and identifies uncertainty/knowledge gap by noting POC testing 'has the potential' to improve health literacy and thus motivates synthesis.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to synthesise the literature regarding POC testing for NCDs and health literacy outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the aim of the review, framing the importance/need to synthesise existing literature on POC testing and health literacy outcomes given the identified relevance to NCD burden and health literacy responsiveness.

No evidence was provided in the retrieved text that discusses existing similar systematic reviews or explains the need for the current review as an update/replication with citation to a previous review.

elements.quote: These findings reflect the potential of POC testing to contribute to more responsive health systems, by improving accessibility, results delivery, and communication of health information.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly describes a mechanism by which the intervention (POC testing) could affect outcomes: improving accessibility, timely results delivery, and communication of health information, which links the intervention to health literacy/system responsiveness.
No retrieved evidence indicates consideration of a logic model or presentation of hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to synthesise the literature regarding POC testing for NCDs and health literacy outcomes.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated in the abstract, but it is not presented using a formal question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO, PICOS, SPIDER).
No statement of planned comparisons using PICO or a similar framework is provided in the available evidence; the manuscript does not describe planned intervention comparisons in PICO format.

elements.quote: Records were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: - (i) the use of at least one POC testing device assessing NCD measures, including cardiovascular disease (e.g. lipid profiles, coagulation markers), chronic respiratory disease (e.g. FeNO), or diabetes (e.g. HbA1c, blood glucose). POC testing was considered across multiple contexts, including adult care, paediatric care, self-managed testing, clinic-based testing, or community health settings; - (ii) reporting of at least one measure related to health literacy or health literacy responsiveness, including outcomes mapped to the five WHO health literacy actions ( Access , Understand , Appraise , Remember , Use ). ... - (iii) health literacy of individuals aged 10 + years, including older children and adolescents, with caregivers able to report their own health literacy outcomes based on POC assessment of a child; - (iv) full-text peer reviewed journal article published within the five years prior to the search. Studies were excluded if they were reviews of peerreviewed studies. The five-year limit was applied in line with WHO guidance to capture contemporary evidence on POC testing and health literacy, reflecting advances in diagnostic technologies and evolving definitions of health literacy. No restrictions on the type of study design, sample size, or language of manuscript were imposed.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies key study characteristics used for eligibility (types of POC tests, clinical contexts/settings, age range, outcomes of interest, study design not restricted). However, it does not specify any follow-up requirements or minimum follow-up duration, so the characteristic 'follow-up requirements' is not addressed.

elements.quote: full-text peer reviewed journal article published within the five years prior to the search. ... No restrictions on the type of study design, sample size, or language of manuscript were imposed.
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria for report characteristics are explicitly stated: a five-year publication window and requirement for full-text peer-reviewed articles, and the manuscript states there were no language restrictions.
No retrieved evidence explicitly distinguishes exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: To address the research question, six studies adopted a qualitative approach, six utilised quantitative methods, and one used mixed methods (Table 1). All outcomes were treated as proxy measures of health literacy or
elements.reason: The review specifies groups used in synthesis (qualitative, quantitative, mixed methods) and, together with Table 1 (table_0) and other text, groups studies by condition/POC test (diabetes, coagulation, mixed/other) and maps outcomes to WHO health literacy actions used for narrative synthesis, thereby linking groupings to the comparisons/objectives.

elements.quote: The five-year limit was applied in line with WHO guidance to capture contemporary evidence on POC testing and health literacy, reflecting advances in diagnostic technologies and evolving definitions of health literacy.
elements.reason: A rationale is provided for the notable restriction of including only studies published within the five years prior to the search (to capture contemporary evidence in line with WHO guidance).

elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the date range and the final date the sources were searched (5 May 2018 to 5 May 2023).

elements.quote: The search strategy was methodologically developed in collaboration with an experienced research librarian, following multiple pilot searches to refine database queries and MeSH terms across several databases to maximise coverage.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes conducting multiple pilot searches to refine queries and MeSH terms, which constitutes a description of validation/refinement of the search strategy.
There is no description of any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or the process/tool used in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The search strategy consisted of MeSH terms including Point-of-Care Testing; Health Promotion; Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice; Patient Education as Topic; Health Literacy; Health Education; Life Style; Diet; Exercise; Health Behaviour; Smoking Cessation; Smoking Reduction; Tobacco Use Cessation; Alcohol Abstinence; Social Behaviour; and Social Participation. Keywords included domains of point-of-care (point of care, bedside, rapid, handheld, remote, mobile), testing (test, screening, diagnosis, monitor), patient (health, informed consent, disease, condition), knowledge (awareness, understanding, competence, comprehension), and behaviour (lifestyle, weight, diet, physical activity, alcohol, social, engage, community, smoking, tobacco).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the conceptual structure used for the search (domains, MeSH terms and keyword groupings), which explains the final conceptual structure and the explorations used to develop it.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity in intervention type (e.g. community screening vs. clinical monitoring), disease focus (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular), outcome measurement tools (e.g. Patient Activation Measure, PAM-13; behaviour change), and population characteristics, which restricted comparability. elements.quote: Meta-analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity in intervention type (e.g. community screening vs. clinical monitoring), disease focus (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular), outcome measurement tools (e.g. Patient Activation Measure, PAM-13; behaviour change), and population characteristics, which restricted comparability. elements.quote: Each outcome was mapped to the domains that best reflected the construct measured, and findings were then categorised by condition and type of POC test.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity in intervention type (e.g. community screening vs. clinical monitoring), disease focus (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular), outcome measurement tools (e.g. Patient Activation Measure, PAM-13; behaviour change), and population characteristics, which restricted comparability. We therefore employed a framework-guided narrative synthesis. Qualitative and quantitative outcome data were extracted and deductively coded against the five WHO health literacy actions ( Access , Understand , Appraise , Remember , Use ) to enable thematic comparison. elements.reason: The authors describe how they prepared data for synthesis: they explain why meta-analysis was not done, that they used a framework-guided narrative synthesis, deductively coded outcomes against WHO domains, mapped outcomes to domains, and categorised findings — but they do not report specific methods for handling missing summary statistics or any data conversions (e.g., imputations, unit conversions), so the description of preparation methods is incomplete.

elements.quote: Although comprehensive, the omission of device-specific and risk-factor terms may have limited retrieval of eligible studies, and citation searching was not undertaken. Future reviews should expand search terms to include specific NCDs, risk factors, and device-specific terminology to ensure broader coverage. ... Included studies were limited to publications from the five years prior to the search, an intentional scope decision aligned with WHO guidance to capture contemporary evidence for POC tests and health literacy definitions. As the final search was conducted in May 2023, the study is limited in its consideration of more recent evidence or developments in POC testing, and the findings should be interpreted as reflecting the evidence base up to that date. Additionally, 11 full-text reports were unable to be retrieved, largely due to being abstract-only or presented in nonwritten formats. While these reports may lack sufficient methodological detail for full appraisal, their exclusion may still introduce retrieval bias and contribute to the narrow evidence base identified. Meta-analysis was not feasible due to variability between interventions, disease focus, measurement tools, and population characteristics. Outcomes were assessed using diverse instruments, ranging from validated tools (e.g. PAM-13) to study-developed questionnaires, qualitative interviews, and clinical markers of adherence or control. This mix of validated and self-reported proxy measures introduces differences in measurement rigour, further limiting comparability across studies. Designs were predominantly cross-sectional or short-term, with limited longitudinal follow-up. Furthermore, equity indicators were inconsistently reported, limiting disaggregated analysis. Although age and sex variables were consistently reported, ethnicity and socioeconomic indicators were often absent, restricting the ability to generalise findings to diverse populations. ... elements.quote: In LMICs, POC testing has particular potential to reduce inequities in the diagnosis, and subsequent prevention, treatment, and care of NCDs. In settings with limited resources, household funds can be quickly depleted by NCD care and treatment, furthering socioeconomic inequities [2]. The introduction of high-impact interventions tailored for implementation in LMICs is therefore imperative.
elements.reason: The authors discuss implications for policy by highlighting POC testing's potential to reduce inequities in LMICs and stating that implementation of tailored, high-impact interventions is imperative, which is a policy-level recommendation.

elements.quote: Expanding future research to include diverse geographies (e.g. LMICs), as well as broader POC tests (e.g. chronic respiratory disease), will strengthen understanding and generalisability, particularly in priority populations. Although some studies utilised validated Patient Activation Measures or assessment of biomarker changes, no identified studies applied specific health literacy measurement tools for outcome assessment. As a key determinant of health, future studies should adopt the use of global health literacy instruments, such as the Health Literacy Questionnaire (HLQ) [36], to generate more targeted data and improve between-study comparisons. Furthermore, longitudinal designs and clarity in reporting equity indicators would benefit future research. Future work may also consider how system-level implementation and responsiveness in scaling up POC testing influence individual health literacy outcomes.
